newsitem.title: USA: Consumer groups ask FTC to bar Shell-Texaco merger.
newsitem.headline: Consumer groups ask FTC to bar Shell-Texaco merger.

text.p: Five consumer groups Friday pressed the Federal Trade Commission to reject the proposed merger of Shell Oil Co and Texaco Inc's western U.S. oil refining and marketing operations.

With fewer and fewer companies operating in West Coast markets and high gasoline prices, "we urge the Commission to block the proposed merger between Shell and Texaco," the groups led by Citizen Action said in a filing to the FTC.

The union of the giant refiners would violate federal merger guidelines, they said, by eliminating the potential for competition between the two, especially in major metropolitan gasoline markets in California, Washington, Oregon and Nevada.

"Furthermore, as competition has declined and the market shares and market power of the few, large, integrated remaining companies have grown, the ability of new companies to enter the market has been severely constrained, especially in California which has imposed new, stricter environmental regulations," the filing said.
The groups said the FTC should also take into consideration "a long history of anticompetitive activity, monopolization and collusion by major oil companies" on the West Coast.

The filing pointed to the decline of independent refiners, especially in the Los Angeles area, where over the last five years the number of independents has fallen from nine with 30 percent of refining capacity to four with just 12 percent.

According to the companies, the merged firm would operate service stations in 28 Midwest and western states with less than 15 percent of national market share and own less than 13 percent of U.S. refining capacity.

But the consumer groups said the FTC should focus on the impact of the merger on local markets. "The relevant markets for refining and retailing are not national markets, but regional and metropolitan markets, respectively," they said.
In the West Coast market, the Shell/Texaco merger would have 23 percent of refining capacity, and about 17 percent of the retail gasoline market.
Combined with their closest competitors, four companies would control more than 80 percent of the refining market and 71 percent of the gasoline market, according to the consumer groups' filing.
The FTC said it is in the process of reviewing the Shell-Texaco merger, but would not comment on how far it was in the process.

In general, the FTC has 30 business days to review a merger after the companies have filed for approval and if the agency asks for more information, it has another 20 days after the extra filings to complete its review. However, additional filings often take months to complete.
A spokeswoman for Texaco said the companies expect federal, state and local reviews of the merger to be completed by the end of this year.
